title: “HE TRIED TO RETURN THE MONEY.”
paragraphs: “HE TRIED TO RETURN THE MONEY.”

Thirty pieces of silver.
Cold.
Heavy.
Loud in his trembling hands.
But the sound that haunted him wasn’t the coins.

It was the rooster.
The silence.
The look on Jesus’ face.
In Gospel of Matthew 27, Judas does something shocking. He confesses.
“I have sinned,” he says. “For I have betrayed innocent blood.” (Matthew 27:4)
Let that sink in.

He knew Jesus was innocent.
He knew he was guilty.
He felt regret burning through his chest like acid.
And he tried to undo it.

He ran back to the religious leaders.
Coins clutched in sweating fists.
Eyes wild.
Voice cracking.
“I don’t want this anymore.”
But religion without repentance has no mercy.
“What is that to us?” they answered. “See to it yourself.”
That’s the coldest line in the chapter.

They wanted his betrayal.
They didn’t want his brokenness.
So Judas threw the money into the temple.
The silver hit the floor like thunder.

But hear me, beloved—
throwing away the money didn’t wash away the sin.
And here’s the tragedy.

Judas had regret.
But he didn’t run to Jesus.
He ran from Him.
There is a difference between remorse and repentance.

Remorse says, “I feel bad.”
Repentance says, “Jesus, save me.”
The Greek word used for Judas’ regret implies deep anguish. Some scholars interpret it as emotional remorse rather than true repentance that turns toward God.
And that difference changes eternity.

Peter denied Jesus three times.
Judas betrayed Him with a kiss.
Both failed.

One wept and ran back to Christ.
One isolated himself in despair.

The enemy loves that space.
The space between guilt and grace.
Judas believed his sin was bigger than the Savior.
And that is the lie hell whispers to every one of us.

“Too far.”
“Too dirty.”
“Too late.”
But look at the cross rising in the same chapter.

While Judas is drowning in regret,
Jesus is walking toward crucifixion.

For betrayers.
For deniers.
For religious hypocrites.
For you.

The silver could not purchase forgiveness.
But the blood of Christ could.
Listen carefully.
If Judas had fallen at Jesus’ feet instead of collapsing under shame, the story could have been different. The cross was sufficient even for him.
That’s how powerful the Gospel is.

Sin is real.
Betrayal is real.
Consequences are real.
But grace is more real.

Regret that runs away becomes despair.
Regret that runs to Jesus becomes redemption.
So what are you holding right now?

A secret?
A compromise?
Thirty pieces of silver in another form?
Don’t just throw it down.
Turn around.
Run to the One you betrayed.
Because the same chapter that records Judas’ regret records Christ’s sacrifice.
And the cross is bigger than your worst decision.
Always.
Come home.
